reviews.title: The Invite
reviews.deck: Olivia Wilde’s full-length directorial debut *Booksmart* (2019) announced her as a strong talent behind the camera.
reviews.author: Chad Durham
reviews.body:
Olivia Wilde’s full-length directorial debut *Booksmart* (2019) announced her as a strong talent behind the camera. Critics and audiences responded well to the funny and reflective movie about teen best friends on the eve of their high school graduation. However, Wilde’s next directorial effort, *Don’t Worry Darling* (2022), though ambitious and starring a great cast, was widely panned and, for some, considered a step back. So it is heartening to see the success and dexterity of her latest. *The Invite* is a humorous, mature, seriously entertaining drama that finds thoughtful things to say about marriage, communication, and keys to understanding others.

The story concerns married couple Joe (Seth Rogen) and Angela (Olivia Wilde), who have a little strain showing in their marriage. Since their daughter is away at a sleepover, Angela has invited the couple who lives above them, Piña (Penelope Cruz) and Hawk (Edward Norton), over for dinner. Once the couples get together, the discussions between these distinct personalities take the night in surprising directions.

The script, from Rashida Jones and Will McCormack (and based on Cesc Gay’s screenplay for *The People Upstairs*) is shrewd. The movie feels like a play, mostly staying in one location–Angela and Joe’s apartment–and hinging almost entirely on dialogue. Though this can often halt a movie’s dynamism, here it narrows the focus with insight. It avoids obvious punchlines, sidesteps clichés, and slyly reveals interesting things about each character and their motivations. Wilde’s direction, as well, is assured, utilizing the cinematography by Adam Newport-Berra to seamlessly enhance the humor and melancholy. They symbolically shoot through windows often, giving the sense that the audience is spying on private things and they deftly employ crucial close-ups to excavate emotion. The camera work never overshadows the story, but serves it productively. And Wilde coaxes disciplined but diverse performances from her talented cast.

Those performances are stellar across the board. Without the principals injecting realism and clarity, the movie would feel much more stagey. Rogen, known as an effective comedic presence, is subtler here and weaponizes his schlubby persona to singular effect. Part of the strength of Joe comes from the audience’s expectations of what Rogen normally portrays. The depth he plumbs here may catch some viewers off-guard. Likewise, Cruz’s role deepens as the movie progresses and she showcases her veteran presence with surprising ease, managing to deliver some of the movie’s biggest themes without a drop of artifice. Norton balances his tone of voice and facial expressions to suggest Hawk’s intriguing vision and confusion. Those are not easy contrasts to adequately convey simultaneously. Finally, Wilde does not let sitting in the director’s chair overshadow her performance in the movie. Angela’s angst and dissatisfaction must feel authentic for the audience to care about her relationship. Wilde’s subtle body language and reasonable reactions connect the audience to her key feelings.

The biggest strength of *The Invite*, ultimately, is its confidence. As every member of the cast imbues their role with realism and depth, every piece of dialogue and turn of the story is calculated for what it reveals about the two couples, and every shot–no matter how simple or showy–seems to have a purpose. It is true that some movies have noticeable conviction unsupported by the flimsiness of what they present. Here, Wilde and her team reveal interesting and rich truths through the accurate belief that they have made something valuable. *The Invite* will last as a comedic and dramatic triumph, likely leading to multiple Oscar nominations.
